references.text: After the Sermon on the Mount, the crowds were amazed at Jesus' teaching, because he taught them as one who had authority, and not as their scribes. This is the closest parallel to Luke 4:32, with the same theme of amazement at Jesus' authoritative teaching.
Mark's parallel account of the event in the synagogue in Capernaum, where the people were amazed at Jesus' teaching because he taught them as one who had authority, and not as the scribes.

After Jesus drives out an unclean spirit, everyone is amazed and says that he teaches with authority and even commands the unclean spirits, and they obey him. This expands on the authority mentioned in Luke 4:32.
The servants who were sent to arrest Jesus came back and said: 'Never has anyone spoken like this man.' This confirms the unique authority of Jesus' words.

Luke's own continuation of the account, where the people are amazed and say that with authority and power Jesus commands the unclean spirits, and they go out. This shows what the authority in his words meant in practice.

Paul urges Titus to speak, exhort, and rebuke with full authority. The concept of authority (ἐξουσία) in the preaching of God's word is a recurring theme that has its source in Jesus' own authoritative teaching.
When Jesus came to his hometown, the people there were amazed at his wisdom and miracles and asked where he got this from. The reaction of amazement at Jesus' teaching is a recurring motif.
Already as a twelve-year-old in the temple, all who heard Jesus were amazed at his understanding and answers. This shows that his authoritative words characterized him from his youth.
